content: These guidelines are informed by a public health approach to scaling up the use of antiviral therapy for hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. This approach aims to ensure the broadest possible access to high-quality services at the population level by employing simplified and standardized methods. It seeks to balance the implementation of the best-proven standards of care with what is feasible on a large scale in resource-limited settings. Access to healthcare is a fundamental human right, applicable equally to men, women, and children, regardless of gender, race, sexual orientation, socioeconomic status, or behavioral practices, including drug use. Promoting human rights and equity in access to HBV prevention, treatment, care, and support is a central principle of these guidelines. Individuals with HBV infection may belong to vulnerable groups due to low socioeconomic status, limited access to appropriate healthcare, or membership in marginalized or stigmatized populations, such as people who inject drugs (PWID), men who have sex with men, migrants, indigenous peoples, or prisoners. HBV treatment programs must prioritize access to treatment for individuals with the most advanced disease who need it most, as well as for pregnant women, children, and vulnerable groups. Treatment should be provided in an environment that minimizes stigma and discrimination. Informed consent must always be obtained, particularly for HBV testing and initiating antiviral therapy. Adequate safeguards must be in place to ensure confidentiality. Countries may face significant challenges in implementing these recommendations for the care and treatment of individuals with chronic hepatitis B (CHB), especially in the context of resource and health system constraints. A key challenge involves prioritizing treatment access for those with the most advanced disease. Each country must develop its own approach to ensure that other care and treatment programs, such as antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV infection, are not disrupted and that expanded access is fair and equitable. The provision of quality screening, care, and treatment for individuals with CHB requires the involvement of appropriately trained personnel and facilities capable of regular monitoring, particularly for those on therapy. The requirements for facilities providing HBV treatment depend on the setting but must include access to appropriate laboratory facilities for monitoring treatment response and adequate supplies of medication. Operating testing services under quality management systems is essential to ensure reliable testing results. Protecting confidentiality and adopting a non-coercive approach are fundamental principles of good clinical practice. The implementation of these guidelines should be informed by the local context, including national HBV epidemiology, health systems and laboratory capacity, drug and commodity supply systems, financial resources, the organization and capacity of the health system, and the anticipated cost-effectiveness of various interventions. Chapter 12 of these guidelines addresses decision-making and planning for the development of hepatitis treatment programs and implementation considerations for key recommendations relevant to country program managers. The WHO guidelines were developed following the recommendations outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2012). A Guidelines Development Group was formed, ensuring representation from various stakeholders, including individuals living with chronic hepatitis, advocacy groups, researchers, clinicians, and program managers. Geographic representation and gender balance were also considered in selecting group members. The group conducted an initial scoping and planning process to formulate questions across the continuum of hepatitis B care and treatment, particularly relevant to lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). These questions were structured in the PICO format (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcomes), and patient-important outcomes were identified, refined, and ranked based on their significance to the patient population. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of primary literature were commissioned externally to address the research questions and patient-important outcomes. The quality of evidence was assessed and rated using the GRADE system, which separates the rating of evidence quality from the strength of recommendations. Evidence quality is classified as high, moderate, low, or very low, with randomized controlled trials (RCTs) initially rated as high-quality evidence but subject to downgrading for factors such as bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, or publication bias. Observational studies are initially rated as low-quality evidence but may be upgraded if the treatment effect is very large, consistent across multiple studies, or demonstrates a dose-response relationship. The strength of a recommendation reflects the confidence that the desirable effects of following the recommendation outweigh the potential undesirable effects. Recommendations are classified as strong or conditional. A strong recommendation indicates high confidence that the benefits outweigh the risks, while a conditional recommendation reflects less certainty about the trade-offs. Conditional recommendations may be adopted by most people or settings but not universally or only under certain conditions. The Guidelines Development Group reviewed evidence profiles, formulated and finalized the wording of recommendations, and evaluated implementation needs. Areas requiring further research were identified. The final recommendations were agreed upon by consensus during a teleconference in July 2014. After addressing comments and questions from group members, a draft document was prepared and circulated for review. Suggested changes were incorporated into subsequent drafts, which were reviewed by the WHO Steering Group and external peer reviewers. The guideline methodologist ensured the appropriate application of the GRADE framework throughout the development process. In accordance with WHO policy, all members of the Guidelines Development Group and peer reviewers completed a Declaration of Interest form. The Secretariat found no cases of exclusive membership in advisory panels or financial conflicts of interest that necessitated exclusion from the guideline development process. The guidelines will be launched in March 2015 at the annual meeting of the Asian Pacific Association for the Study of the Liver, which gathers approximately 5,000 individuals involved in hepatitis care. They will also be accessible on the WHO website, translated into official UN languages, and supported by additional tools for country implementation. The implementation of these guidelines will be assessed by the number of countries incorporating them into their national treatment guidelines. Future monitoring will focus on the number of individuals treated for CHB, although no national-level monitoring system currently exists to collect this information. Hepatitis B infection is caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV), an enveloped DNA virus that infects the liver and causes hepatocellular necrosis and inflammation. HBV infection can be acute or chronic, ranging from asymptomatic or mild disease to severe or fulminant hepatitis. Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) infection is defined as the persistent presence of detectable hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) in the blood or serum for longer than six months, with or without active viral replication and evidence of hepatocellular injury and inflammation. Chronicity is common following acute infection in neonates (90% of those born to HBeAg-positive mothers) and young children under five years of age (20–60%) but occurs rarely (<5%) when infection is acquired in adulthood.
